claims.text: The Liskov Substitution Principle: code that uses a base type must work correctly, without change, when given objects of any of its subtypes.
claims.source_hint: glossary entry lsp; standard formulation in software design literature

claims.text: ShippingFee declares abstract int ForOrder(int totalVnd); StandardShipping returns 0 from 2,000,000 else 30,000, ExpressShipping 60,000, PickUpInStore 0 — each returns an int for every int input and none throws.

ShippingFeeBase declares abstract int ForOrder(int totalVnd); StandardShippingOk returns 0 from 2,000,000 else 30,000; BulkOnlyShipping returns 45,000 from 5,000,000 and throws InvalidOperationException("order too small for bulk shipping") below.
The C# compiler checks that an override matches the base method's parameters and return type; C# has no checked exceptions, so it does not check whether a method throws for some inputs.
claims.source_hint: C# language reference: override; C# has no checked exceptions

claims.text: EveryKindAnswersTheSameCall builds a ShippingFee[] of the three kinds and asserts that ForOrder(2_000_000) on each gives {0, 60000, 0}.

Hand trace: StandardShippingOk.ForOrder(500_000) = 30000, (6_000_000) = 0; BulkOnlyShipping.ForOrder(6_000_000) = 45000, (500_000) throws InvalidOperationException "order too small for bulk shipping".
A test calling BulkOnlyShipping.ForOrder only with 5,000,000 would get 45,000 and pass, so a passing test at one value does not show the subtype keeps the promise for all values.
Implementing every abstract method is enforced by the C# compiler (CS0534); LSP concerns behaviour beyond that.
claims.source_hint: C# compiler error CS0534; outline misconception 1

claims.text: A subtype that throws for inputs the base type's method accepts breaks substitution: callers written for the base type are no longer correct for it.
claims.source_hint: outline item 3; follows from the LSP definition
